extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, literary studies, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating the technical means and tendencies of wit as described in a psychoanalytic/literary treatment of humor (techniques, examples, and purposes). Useful for analysing or producing witty material informed by Freud's categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion (indirect expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusion is perhaps the commonest and most easily employed means of wit; I have sometimes called allusion 'indirect expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusion by itself is not necessarily witty; only those allusions which 'show a “witty” element' count as wit. Allusion functions as substitution or indirect representation (symbolism, trifle, or reference) and is a central technique of word- and thought-wit. Anti-pattern: mere reference or phraseological allusion that lacks a distinct witty operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the minute/minutest element
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation through a minute or minutest element: solving the problem by bringing the entire character to full expression through a minute detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a trivial or tiny detail closely connected to the subject to stand for and reveal the whole character or situation (examples: the Jew on the train putting feet back when asked about Yom Kippur; the physician waiting until the unmistakable cry to act). Technique allied to the economy tendency—condenses character into a small sign. Scoring note: effectiveness depends on the clarity of the association between the small detail and the larger character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison (as indirect expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison is another kind of indirect expression used in wit, but whether a comparison is truly witty is often doubtful and problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons can produce wit by (a) restoring force to a fixed phrase via further building/deduction, (b) creating unexpected continuations/unification, or (c) by producing absurd or striking attributions. Examples: Lichtenberg's 'torch of truth' expanded to 'singeing somebody’s beard'; continuing a comparison often creates the witty effect. Anti-pattern: a bland or overused comparison that lacks further inventive development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation/Unification of a comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing or expanding a comparison to establish an unexpected association (unification) can produce wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comparison that is extended or unified with related imagery can create a witty deduction or association (e.g., comparing reviews to children's diseases and continuing the analogy). The witty element often comes from linking the initial metaphor to further consequences within the same analogy. Scoring: witty when extension yields surprise or a new, coherent mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through absurdity / peculiar attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit often arises from absurd or peculiar attributions revealed by a comparison (e.g., 'the learned bowels of the writers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create attributes or combinations that are strikingly incongruous or absurd; the absurd attribute itself can carry the wit. Examples include degrading or debasing comparisons that juxtapose high abstractions with low concrete images (e.g., 'pants of good-breeding'). Anti-pattern: gratuitous vulgarity without an incongruous cognitive mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debasement/degrading comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing an abstraction of high category beside a very concrete or low thing (debasing) can contribute to the witty effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the shock/value-difference between abstract/high and concrete/low to produce humor (examples: 'buttons tore from the pants of my patience'). Beware that debasement is a particular rhetorical choice and may be offensive depending on audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application of the same material (word-play / sound-play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the same verbal material repeatedly with peculiar modifications (play on words, sound similarity) is a technique of word-wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques like 'shake-up' rhymes or puns (e.g., 'Dame Luck' → 'Lame Duck', 'Home-Roulard' for Home Rule) exploit repetition and alteration of the same lexical item for pleasure. Scoring: clarity of linguistic pivot and economy of expression increase effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation with substitutive formation (nucleus of word-wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation with substitutive formation is identified as the nucleus of the technique of word-wit and is akin to dream-formation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense multiple associations into one compact expression or substitute one element for another to create a compact, layered meaning. This is psychologically linked to dream mechanisms; effective when listeners can (often unconsciously) resolve the condensation into its elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-wit mechanisms: displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement is a technique of thought-wit whereby emphasis or affect is shifted from one idea to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displacement to transfer psychic intensity to an unexpected element, producing surprise or incongruity. Displacement is one of the shared mechanisms between wit and dream-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-wit mechanisms: faulty thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Faulty thinking (errors of thought) is a mechanism used in thought-wit to create comic or witty outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design jokes that hinge on slips, mistaken inferences, or logical errors in reasoning; these mimic thought-wit processes and can yield wit when the audience recognizes the error and the implied insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-wit mechanisms: indirect expression (allusion/symbolism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect expression—substitution by allusion, trifle, or symbolism analogous to comparison—is a common thought-wit mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encode thoughts in indirect forms so that the witty meaning emerges by association rather than explicit statement. Examples include symbolism or small signs standing for larger meanings; effectiveness relies on audience's associative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation through the opposite (contradiction or reversal) is a common technique in wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce wit by stating or implying opposites or reversals that reveal an unexpected relation or critique; this technique parallels dream mechanisms and contributes to displacement/absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy (tendency to economize expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency of economy—expressing much by little—is a recurring element in the technique of word-wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, economical formulations where a small verbal device or detail yields disproportionate expressive effect (ties to representation-through-minute and condensation). Scoring: greater economy often correlates with stronger witty effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless (abstract) wit versus Tendency (purposive) wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'harmless' (abstract) wit that exists for its own sake and 'tendency' wit which serves a purpose (e.g., satire, aggression, seduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmless wit aims mainly at pleasure and can be shallow or profound; tendency-wit has an agenda and may offend. These are independent of whether the technique is word- or thought-based. Evaluators should identify whether a joke's purpose is purely aesthetic or instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile wit (satire, aggression, defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency-wit used as aggression, satire, or defense; wit that has a hostile purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hostile wit leverages techniques of wit for attack or social critique; it often produces stronger, more explosive laughter but risks ruffling those targeted. Consider ethical/audience consequences when producing hostile wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscene (smutty) wit as sexual exhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene or smutty jokes intentionally bring sexual facts or relations into prominence and serve as a form of sexual exhibition or attempted seduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: directed toward a person who is the object of sexual excitement; can produce excitation or shame; includes sexual and excrementitious domains (infantile sexual concepts). The smutty joke functions as denudation—forcing the audience to picture sexual parts or acts. Use with caution: social inhibitions and audience norms determine acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure of wit derives from technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure experienced in wit is supplied by the technical means of wit-work (condensation, displacement, indirect expression, etc.), not solely by thought-content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witty wording is replaced by plain wording preserving sense, the wit and laughability are often lost. Therefore, attention to form/technique (not just clever content) is essential in producing humor. Evaluation should distinguish content quality from technical wit-activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity/doubt in classifying comparisons as witty
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons often present greater uncertainty about whether they are genuinely witty compared to other techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when labeling comparisons as wit; examine secondary attributes (absurdity, continuation, allusion) and the quality of the technique. Some comparisons strike as witty because of associated thought-content rather than intrinsic verbal operation.
